B2.title: New Strategy for Solar Cells
B2.body: Researchers from several top institutions in Beijing have made a significant breakthrough in developing tandem solar cells. They created a coordination-regulated strategy to improve the stability of wide-bandgap perovskites, which are used in tandem with narrow-bandgap materials like silicon. These perovskites are crucial for achieving high efficiency in solar cells, but they have a major flaw: they are not very stable. When exposed to light or heat, the halide ions in the perovskites start to move around, causing the material to degrade. This degradation leads to a loss of efficiency and a shorter lifespan for the solar cell. The researchers found that the instability is caused by undercoordinated lead sites, which act as recombination centers and facilitate the migration of halide ions. By addressing this issue, the team hopes to create more efficient and longer-lasting solar cells. The new strategy has the potential to overcome the limitations of current solar cells and pave the way for more widespread adoption of renewable energy. This breakthrough is important because it could lead to more efficient use of solar energy, which is essential for reducing our reliance on fossil fuels. The researchers' work is a significant step forward in the development of tandem solar cells, and it could have a major impact on the future of renewable energy.

C1.title: Perovskites Stabilized for Solar Cells
C1.body: A team of researchers from esteemed institutions, including the Beijing Institute of Technology and the National Institute of Clean-and-Low-Carbon Energy, has devised a novel coordination-regulated strategy aimed at enhancing the phase stability of wide-bandgap (WBG) perovskites. These perovskites are integral to the development of high-efficiency tandem solar cells, where they are utilized as top absorbers in tandem architectures alongside narrow-bandgap materials such as crystalline silicon and Cu(In,Ga)Se2 (CIGS). The incorporation of WBG perovskites in these architectures enables the attainment of efficiencies that surpass the limitations of single-junction devices. However, the inherent instability of WBG perovskites, which typically stems from their mixed-halide compositions, poses a significant challenge. Under prolonged illumination or thermal stress, the migration of halide ions leads to the formation of iodine-rich and bromine-rich domains, resulting in bandgap inhomogeneity, increased non-radiative recombination, and accelerated device degradation. The underlying cause of this instability is closely tied to defect chemistry, with undercoordinated Pb2+ sites playing a pivotal role. These sites not only act as recombination centers but also reduce the formation energy of halide vacancies, which serve as migration pathways for halide ions and facilitate ion redistribution and phase segregation. By addressing the fundamental issue of defect formation during crystallization, the researchers' coordination-regulated strategy offers a promising solution to stabilize WBG perovskites, thereby paving the way for the development of more efficient tandem solar cells. This breakthrough has significant implications for the field of solar energy, as it could lead to the creation of solar cells with enhanced efficiency and durability. The strategy devised by the researchers has the potential to mitigate the limitations associated with WBG perovskites, ultimately contributing to the advancement of solar cell technology.
